params.question: A patient has anaemia with an MCV of 92 fL (normocytic range), yet the peripheral blood smear shows two distinct red cell populations — one microcytic and one macrocytic. Which additional index would best reveal this mixed deficiency?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MCH reflects the average haemoglobin content per cell. Like MCV, it is an averaged value and would not distinguish two distinct cell populations coexisting in the same sample.

Correct. RDW measures the variation in red cell size (anisocytosis). A high RDW with a normal MCV strongly suggests two populations — for example, small iron-deficient cells and large B12-deficient cells averaging out to a normal MCV.
MCHC measures the average haemoglobin concentration within red cells. It is useful for detecting spherocytosis (raised MCHC) but does not reveal variation in cell size across the population.
Haematocrit reflects the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells. It helps quantify the degree of anaemia but provides no information about variation in red cell size.

overallFeedback.feedback: When iron and B12 deficiency coexist, microcytes and macrocytes average out to a normal MCV. The RDW captures this hidden variation by measuring the spread in red cell sizes — it is the key to unmasking mixed deficiencies.
A high RDW alongside a normal MCV is the hallmark of mixed deficiency — always check RDW when the MCV seems unexpectedly normal in a patient with anaemia.

params.question: In the etiological classification of anaemia, a low reticulocyte count in an anaemic patient points to which category of cause?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In haemolysis, the bone marrow accelerates red cell production to compensate for peripheral destruction. This raises the reticulocyte count, often markedly — a low count argues against haemolysis.

After acute haemorrhage, the marrow mounts a compensatory reticulocyte response within 3–5 days. A persistently low count during this window indicates inadequate marrow function, not a normal recovery pattern.

Correct. A low reticulocyte count means the marrow is not generating red cells fast enough — this is the hypoproliferative pattern, seen in iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, aplastic anaemia, and renal erythropoietin deficiency.

answers.text: Chronic blood loss with intact iron stores

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic blood loss eventually depletes iron stores, impairing marrow production. A low reticulocyte count in this setting specifically reflects the production failure component — the marrow cannot compensate because substrate (iron) is lacking.

overallFeedback.feedback: A low reticulocyte count tells you the bone marrow is underperforming. High reticulocytes point to destruction or loss (the marrow is trying); low reticulocytes point to production failure (the marrow cannot keep up).
The reticulocyte count is the marrow's report card. Low count (RPI < 2) = production failure. High count (RPI > 2) = the marrow is working but cells are being destroyed or lost faster.

params.question: In a patient with severe anaemia (haemoglobin 7.5 g/dL), a raw reticulocyte count of 4% confirms that the bone marrow is mounting an adequate compensatory response.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The raw reticulocyte percentage is misleading in anaemia. Because the total red cell count is reduced, even a normal marrow output produces a falsely high percentage. In this example, a 4% raw count corrects to an RPI of just 1.0 after accounting for the degree of anaemia and shift-cell maturation time. An RPI below 2 indicates a hypoproliferative state — the marrow is not keeping up.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is a common trap. The raw reticulocyte percentage is falsely elevated in anaemia because it is calculated against a reduced total red cell count. After correcting for the degree of anaemia and the maturation factor (shift-cell correction), the Reticulocyte Production Index in this example drops to 1.0 — well below the threshold of 2 that indicates adequate marrow compensation.

params.question: In the case of a 55-year-old woman with confirmed iron deficiency anaemia and hookworm eggs on stool examination, why does the video stress that colonoscopy is still indicated?

answers.text: Hookworm infestation rarely causes significant iron loss

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hookworm is a well-established cause of chronic intestinal blood loss and iron deficiency, particularly in rural India. The issue is not that hookworm is insignificant — it is that a second, more serious pathology may coexist.

answers.text: Two causes of iron deficiency can coexist, and gastrointestinal malignancy must be excluded in this age group

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In any post-menopausal woman or adult male, new iron deficiency anaemia requires exclusion of gastrointestinal malignancy regardless of other findings. Hookworm and a colonic carcinoma can coexist — finding one cause must not end the investigation.

answers.text: Stool examination for hookworm ova has a high false-positive rate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stool microscopy for hookworm ova is a reliable diagnostic test. The reason colonoscopy is still needed is not diagnostic uncertainty about hookworm, but the possibility that a second pathology coexists alongside it.

answers.text: Colonoscopy is needed to determine the species of hookworm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hookworm species identification (Ancylostoma duodenale vs Necator americanus) is done by stool microscopy, not colonoscopy. Colonoscopy is indicated here to exclude gastrointestinal malignancy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical principle: one diagnosis does not exclude another. Iron deficiency in a post-menopausal woman or adult male always requires colonoscopy to exclude malignancy, even when another cause such as hookworm or NSAID use has been identified.
Finding hookworm does not end the investigation. In a post-menopausal woman, new iron deficiency anaemia always warrants exclusion of gastrointestinal malignancy — two causes can coexist.
